title: Using machine learning to predict future foster care admission.
ehr_evidence: We make use of data from CareSource Ohio, a nonprofit health plan with the largest Medicaid enrollment in the state of Ohio.
summary: Machine learning predictive modeling study using Medicaid claims and social determinants of health data to identify children at risk of future foster care admission.
key_findings: The gradient-boosted tree model classified 2408 children as at risk, with 1599 (66.4%) actually transitioning into foster care.
The SDOH model achieved a positive predictive value (PPV) of 84.72%, compared to 27.44% for the non-SDOH model.
Logistic regression yielded a PPV of 0% without SDOH variables and 12.7% with SDOH variables, both substantially worse than the gradient-boosted tree model.
Average precision was 0.75 for the SDOH model and 0.16 for the non-SDOH model.
captured_features: linked parental adult diagnoses and utilization
Johns Hopkins ACG System health analytics scores
21 SDOH risk scores (geographic and household-level factors)
study_design: Predictive modeling study comparing gradient-boosted tree machine learning to logistic regression
population: Children under 18 years enrolled in CareSource Medicaid plan in Ohio (2019-2022), with linked parental adult data
exposure_domain: Social determinants of health (SDOH) and clinical/healthcare utilization factors
limitations: Potential missing foster care admissions due to enrollment in different health plans
Model may not generalize to demographically or clinically distinct populations
Lack of sibling status data preventing proper training/validation split
Risk of replicating racial, disability, and socioeconomic biases in the existing child welfare system
